doc.title: Jean Bach interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Ellington as a poor radio guest and 'Honest Ellington'
summary: Ellington was stilted on the show; she recalls his outrageous compliments and his claim to tell the truth.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Yes, absolutely. And the reading of course was a killer, because Arlene never had time to do anything, so I did all the reading. And it got so toward the end that I would say to the publishers, because they knew that we sold books. We had the number one rating on the air and the station was easy to find, right in the middle of the dial, and the loudest station on the dial. And so they’d say, “Oh Jean, this is right up your alley. This book is marvelous. It’s an overview of—” I’d say, “what’s the magic number?” If it was over 300 pages I’d kind of, I figured, I can’t get this read in a night. I did take a reading course, yeah, but not every day. But I did have some jazz people on. But you know a lot of jazz people were horrible guests. Ellington was the worst. And as well as I knew him, and I knew I’d be a better guest talking about him than he was. He was sort of stilted and didn’t give very much, and laughed a lot. Everything was discounted with a laugh. Well Arlene had the same problem. She’d have a question that she didn’t quite believe in, like, “why do men like war?” And then she’d nullify it by going [laughs] like I’m really kidding. So he did a lot of that. So I was out in Milwaukee with a bunch of Ellington fans. And one of them had taped this show. And he said, “what was wrong with Arlene that day?” I said, © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-
“it wasn’t only Arlene, it was Ellington. The two of them were jiving each other and you didn’t get anything. It was not one of his finer moments.
That’s interesting because he was so smooth and debonair in person but it didn’t translate.

But he held information back and he didn’t tell the truth you know. When I was 18, I was a size 18. I was fat, I was awkward, I had no poise — well I still don’t have too much poise, but I was really uugh, it was terrible. And he said to me, because he knew he had me going, I believed everything he said. He said, “you know I’d like you to do something for me.” Oh by now I had a job on a newspaper, that was it. So he told everybody that Eleanor Roosevelt and I were his two favorite writers. I thought gee, that’s great, he likes my writing. So he said, “I wish you’d write a lyric to ‘Sophisticated Lady.’” I said, “I think there is a lyric to ‘Sophisticated Lady.’” He said, “yeah but it’s not right.” He said, “you see you’re my idea of a real sophisticated lady.” And I absolutely believed him. So crazy. He would say things, as I say, as outrageous as these compliments, and I bought every one. But most people did. They wanted to believe it. And then if it got too crazy, and you’d say, “oh come on, you’ve got to be kidding.” He’d say, “well I know it sounds ridiculous, it sounds too far fetched,” but he said, “I have to say it because it’s the truth.” He said, “that’s me, Honest Ellington.” He’s just told you that he knew you were walking because the walls were beginning to tingle that you were going to walk in the room you know. And so Honest Ellington, you know? I can’t keep it back. I have to tell the truth.
